title: Illness
hookLine: praying, seeking medicine, and trusting are not opposites

lines: A ROSARY AND A MEDICATION LIST.
TRUST GOD, OR SEE THE DOCTOR?
THE ANSWER IS IN ORDINARY VERSES.
cards: A hospital waiting room. A woman holds a rosary in one hand and a list of her husband's medications in the other.
Across from her, a man reads the side effects on a pill bottle, then closes his eyes for a moment, lips moving. Nobody in that room thinks they have to choose.
Yet the question comes up in some families: if you really trusted God, would you need the doctor? And if you go to the doctor, were the prayers just for show? Some ordinary Bible verses speak to it.

teach.b: You first heard this at Levi's table. When critics asked why Jesus ate with sinners, he answered: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick."

He used doctors as his picture of help that's needed, not a lack of faith. The letter of James tells the sick to call the elders of the church: "let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
King Hezekiah, sick to the point of death, hears through Isaiah: "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears."
Then the prophet calls for something from the kitchen: "Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaster upon the boil."

teach.h: A PRAYER HEARD, A POULTICE OF FIGS.
teach.b: Prayer heard, and a poultice on the sore.

teach.h: A LITTLE WINE, A BELOVED PHYSICIAN.
teach.b: Paul tells his young friend Timothy, in the King James words, "use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities." Practical advice, in the middle of scripture.
And to the Colossians he names a companion: "Luke, the beloved physician." Tradition holds that this same Luke wrote one of the Gospels. A doctor, counted among the friends of the church.
Now what this doesn't promise. Christians who pray for healing don't all mean the same thing by it. Some expect dramatic recoveries and pray boldly for them.

Others pray mostly for strength, peace and good doctors. Some churches anoint the sick as a sacrament; others lay on hands, or simply pray. What the texts keep doing is holding prayer and care together.

teach.h: HANDS THAT PRAY, HANDS THAT BANDAGE.
teach.b: Hands that pray, and hands that bandage.

how: Christians pray for the sick, by name in services and privately, while also seeking medical care; some churches anoint the sick with oil, following the letter of James, and Catholic and Orthodox churches keep this as a sacrament.

o: a state of the soul that medicine can't touch
a sign someone's prayers weren't strong enough
a weakness of the body, met with prayer and care

games.q: illness in the Bible — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus treated needing a doctor as a lack of faith
he used the physician as his picture of needed help, and Paul calls Luke the beloved physician.
when King Hezekiah was sick, Isaiah called for a lump of figs
his prayer was heard, and the figs were laid on the boil as a plaster.
all Christians mean the same thing when they pray for healing
some pray boldly for recovery, others mainly for strength and good doctors; churches anoint, lay on hands, or simply pray.

games.q: you're one of the early Christians, and someone in your community is sick. according to the letter of James, what should they do?
o: keep quiet and wait it out alone.
call the elders, who pray and anoint them with oil.
avoid the church until they're well.
games.why: James says the sick should call the elders, who pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord. illness is brought into the community, not hidden.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your body that needs care right now: a pill you take, a sore back, a checkup you've been putting off, a night of sleep you keep skipping.
Hold it without judging yourself, and if you pray, name it to God, the way the sick in James are told to. Then choose one plain, practical step for it, and hold the two side by side.

wordCard.voice: Illness. A weakness of the body that the Bible meets with prayer and with practical care, a physician and an anointing, held together.

orig.note: Greek: physician, the word in "they that are whole need not a physician" and in "Luke, the beloved physician."

carryVoice: Your line: both, not either. A pill and a prayer can share a morning. That's today, done.
